title: The Myth of the Thirteen Tribes
summary: The familiar thirteen-tribes list is a useful clue in older sources but a misleading map of Native political life, kinship, and land relationships on Long Island.
content:
Why the list persists

Many books, maps, and classroom summaries divide Native Long Island into thirteen tribes. The list is familiar because it is simple, memorable, and tied to nineteenth-century local history writing. It gathers names that appear in deeds and place-name records, but it should not be treated as a precise political map.

What the list leaves out

Long Island Native communities were connected through villages, kinship, marriage, seasonal movement, waterways, diplomacy, sachems, sunksquaws, and shared responsibilities to land and water. Those relationships changed over time, especially as Dutch and English colonists pushed land transactions, tribute, warfare, disease, and court systems into Native life.

Colonial categories and land pressure

Colonial officials preferred to deal with named leaders and bounded groups because written deeds needed sellers, witnesses, and territories. That made flexible community networks look like fixed tribes with simple borders. Later historians repeated those categories, and the older maps made the structure seem older and more stable than the evidence supports.

How to use older maps responsibly

Older tribal lists are still useful when read carefully. They preserve names that matter, point to regions of memory, and show how colonial records described Native people. A stronger public reading asks what source produced the name, what purpose the record served, and what relationships the map leaves out.

Continuity beyond the myth

Correcting the myth does not erase Native communities. Native Long Island is a network of living peoples, homelands, families, and political histories rather than a frozen set of past-tense labels.

Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

Why is the idea that Long Island had exactly thirteen tribes misleading?

The familiar list of thirteen tribes is a later historical model, not a complete map of fixed pre-contact governments or borders. Many names in colonial records identify places, local communities, or negotiating groups connected through kinship and shared land use.

Silas Wood's 1824 history helped popularize a list of thirteen Long Island tribes that later appeared in books and classroom maps. The list can be a reference point, but it becomes misleading when treated as a precise pre-contact political map. Colonial deeds recorded names for places, local communities, kin groups, and negotiating parties through European legal categories. John A. Strong's research emphasizes more fluid networks of kinship, marriage, leadership, seasonal use, and shared resources. The project therefore presents the thirteen-name model as one layer in the history of interpretation, not as a final description of Indigenous political life.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, pp. 20-21, 24.
  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), p. 308.
  • John A. Strong, Wyandanch and the Dispossession of Indian Land on Long Island, p. 1.
